claim: In embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), >70% of patients retain wild-type TP53.
source: In ERMS, >70% of patients retain wild-type TP53, yet mutations when present are associated with worse prognosis.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that cites established knowledge about TP53 status in ERMS patients.

claim: TP53 mutations in ERMS are associated with worse prognosis.
source: In ERMS, >70% of patients retain wild-type TP53, yet mutations when present are associated with worse prognosis.
evidence: This statement references established clinical observations about TP53 mutations and prognosis.

claim: tp53 loss expands tumor initiation from <35% to >97% of animals in the kRASG12D-driven ERMS model.
source: We demonstrate that tp53 is a major suppressor of tumorigenesis, where tp53 loss expands tumor initiation from <35% to >97% of animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing tumor initiation rates.

claim: TP53C176F partially retains wild-type p53 apoptotic activity.
source: Characterizing three patient-specific alleles reveals that TP53C176F partially retains wild-type p53 apoptotic activity that can be exploited
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing apoptotic activity in tumors expressing TP53C176F.

claim: TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C encode two structurally related proteins with gain-of-function effects that predispose to head musculature ERMS.
source: whereas TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C encode two structurally related proteins with gain-of-function effects that predispose to head musculature ERMS.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling and experimental data showing increased head tumor formation.

claim: TP53P153Δ predisposes to hedgehog-expressing medulloblastomas in the kRASG12D-driven ERMS-model.
source: TP53P153Δ unexpectedly also predisposes to hedgehog-expressing medulloblastomas in the kRASG12D-driven ERMS-model.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data and histological analysis showing medulloblastoma formation.

claim: TP53 is mutated or functionally disrupted in more than 50% of human tumors.
source: TP53 is the best-known tumor suppressor protein that is mutated or functionally disrupted in more than 50% of human tumors (Kastenhuber and Lowe, 2017; Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Germline mutations in TP53 are responsible for Li–Fraumeni syndrome.
source: Germline mutations in TP53 are responsible for Li–Fraumeni syndrome that predisposes to a wide but distinct spectrum of tumors that varies with age (Malkin, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TP53 mutations are correlated with an increased risk of developing RMS and a worse prognosis.
source: Recent studies looking at TP53 alterations in rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) patients show that TP53 mutations are correlated with an increased risk of developing RMS and a worse prognosis (Casey et al., 2021; Shern et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: TP53 mutations are present in >40% of adult carcinomas.
source: TP53 mutations are present in >40% of adult carcinomas and thought to play a major role in tumorigenesis (Gröbner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mutations in TP53 are found in less than 6% of pediatric cancers.
source: In contrast, mutations in TP53 are found in less than 6% of pediatric cancers (Chen et al., 2014a; Chen, 2013; Gröbner et al., 2018; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014; Tirode et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In human ERMS, the TP53 locus is mutated or deleted in 16% of tumors.
source: For example, in human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), a common pediatric cancer of muscle, the TP53 locus is mutated or deleted in 16% of tumors, while transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of tumors, either through direct locus disruption or MDM2 amplification (Chen, 2013; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TP53 transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of ERMS tumors.
source: For example, in human embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS), a common pediatric cancer of muscle, the TP53 locus is mutated or deleted in 16% of tumors, while transcriptional activity is altered in >30% of tumors, either through direct locus disruption or MDM2 amplification (Chen, 2013; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TP53 mutations are detected in ERMS at relapse.
source: TP53 mutations are also detected in ERMS at relapse, suggesting a role in tumor progression and/or resistance to therapy (Chen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and suggests an inference about the role in progression.

claim: tp53del/del (tp53-/-) zebrafish spontaneously developed a spectrum of tumors including MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive natural killer cell-like leukemia.
source: tp53del/del (tp53-/-) zebrafish spontaneously developed a spectrum of tumors that includes malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors (MPNSTs), angiosarcomas, germ cell tumors, and an aggressive natural killer cell-like leukemia (Ignatius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: tp53 loss does not change the overall frequency of ERMS self-renewing cancer stem cells.
source: The role for tp53 in self-renewal and metastasis of kRASG12D-induced ERMS tumors was assessed using cell transplantation assays and revealed that tp53 loss does not change the overall frequency of ERMS self-renewing cancer stem cells compared to tumors expressing wild-type tp53 (Ignatius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: tp53-/- ERMS were more invasive and metastatic compared to tp53 wild-type tumors.
source: In contrast, tp53-/- ERMS were more invasive and metastatic compared to tp53 wild-type tumors, providing new insights into how tp53 suppresses ERMS progression in vivo (Ignatius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Co-injection of rag2:kRASG12D and rag2:DsRed resulted in approximately 34% of tp53+/+ animals with DsRed-positive tumors by 60 d post injection.
source: Co-injection of rag2:kRASG12D and rag2:DsRed resulted in approximately 34% of tp53+/+ animals (n = 49/143 animals) with DsRed-positive tumors by 60 d post injection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Up to 97% of tp53-/- animals displayed tumors by 60 d in the kRASG12D-driven ERMS model.
source: In stark contrast, up to 97% of tp53-/- animals displayed tumors (n = 139/142 animals) by 60 d.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: kRASG12D-induced tp53-/- ERMS displayed a very rapid onset, with the majority arising within the first 20 d of life.
source: kRASG12D-induced tp53-/- ERMS displayed a very rapid onset, with the majority of arising within the first 20 d of life (Figure 1A; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: tp53-/- mutant ERMS displayed a significant increase in size compared to tp53+/+ animals.
source: We assessed tumor size and the number of tumors initiated and found that tp53-/- mutant ERMS displayed a significant increase in size (Figure 1B and D; p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claim: tp53-/- mutant ERMS displayed a significant increase in the number of tumors per animal compared to tp53+/+ animals.
source: We assessed tumor size and the number of tumors initiated and found that tp53-/- mutant ERMS displayed a significant increase in size (Figure 1B and D; p<0.0001) and in the number of tumors per animal (Figure 1B and C; p<0.0001) compared to tp53+/+ animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Histological assessment showed no major differences between tp53+/+ and tp53-/- ERMS.
source: Histological assessment showed no major differences between tp53+/+ and tp53-/- ERMS, and tumors formed in the head, trunk, or tail similarly in both backgrounds (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Tumors formed in the head, trunk, or tail similarly in both tp53+/+ and tp53-/- backgrounds.
source: Histological assessment showed no major differences between tp53+/+ and tp53-/- ERMS, and tumors formed in the head, trunk, or tail similarly in both backgrounds (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: tp53-/- and tp53+/+ ERMS have similar expression levels of kRASG12D and dusp4.
source: We assessed relative expression of kRASG12D and its downstream effector dusp4 in tumors from tp53-/- and tp53+/+ zebrafish and confirmed similar expression levels of kRASG12D and dusp4 using quantitative qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; n = 3 tumors each, p=0.8966 unpaired t-test with Welch's correction).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: tp53 is a major suppressor of tumor initiation in RAS-driven zebrafish ERMS.
source: Taken together, our analysis suggests that tp53 is a major suppressor of tumor initiation in RAS-driven zebrafish ERMS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: tp53-/- tumors displayed a significant increase in EdU-positive cells compared to tp53 wild-type ERMS sections.
source: EdU analyses revealed that tp53-/- tumors displayed a significant increase in EdU-positive cells (Figure 2A; p<0.0001 Student's t-test)
evidence: This is supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: tp53-/- tumors displayed significantly more phospho-histone H3-expressing cells compared to tp53 wild-type ERMS sections.
source: and significantly more phospho-histone H3-expressing cells when compared to tp53 wild-type ERMS sections (Figure 2B; p<0.01 Student's t-test), indicating increased proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-histone H3 staining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Annexin V staining showed no significant difference in the rate of late apoptosis between tp53-/- and wild-type ERMS.
source: Annexin V staining showed no significant difference in the rate of late apoptosis (Q2) (Figure 2C–E; p=0.592 Student's t-test)
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: tp53-/- mutant ERMS showed a small yet significant decrease in early apoptosis compared to wild-type.
source: but showed a small yet significant decrease in early apoptosis (Q4) in tp53-/- mutant ERMS compared to wild-type (Figure 2C–E; p=0.0073 Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: tp53 is a potent suppressor of kRAS-induced ERMS tumor cell proliferation, with only a moderate effect on apoptosis.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that tp53 is a potent suppressor of kRAS-induced ERMS tumor cell proliferation, with only a moderate effect on apoptosis, affecting ERMS initiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on proliferation and apoptosis.

claim: Zebrafish and human p53 share 56% identity with respect to amino acid sequence.
source: Zebrafish and human p53 are functionally similar and share 56% identity with respect to amino acid sequence (67% positives, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Berghmans et al., 2005; Ignatius et al., 2018; Parant et al., 2010; Storer and Zon, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figure supplement and citations.

claim: Within the core DNA-binding region of p53, 72% conservation exists between zebrafish and human.
source: Within the core DNA-binding region where a majority of mutations occur in patients, 72% conservation exists (79% positives, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figure supplements.

claim: Co-expression of kRASG12D along with TP53WT significantly suppressed tumor initiation in tp53-/- zebrafish.
source: Co-expression of kRASG12D along with TP53WT significantly suppressed tumor initiation (Figure 3A; p<0.0001, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ERMS in TP53WT-expressing animals were smaller than tumors in age-matched tp53-/- zebrafish.
source: ERMS in TP53WT-expressing animals were smaller than tumors in age-matched tp53-/- zebrafish (Figure 3B and C; p<0.0001 Student's t-test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of ERMS initiated per zebrafish between tp53-/- and tp53-/- + TP53WT groups.
source: however, we observed no significant difference in the number or distribution of ERMS initiated per zebrafish between the two groups (Figure 3D and E; p=0.065 for Figure 3D, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Co-expressing TP53WT significantly inhibited proliferation in ERMS tumors.
source: Analysis of EdU staining of ERMS tumors determined that co-expressing TP53WT significantly inhibited proliferation (Figure 3F; p=0.0007 Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: An overall increase in the number of apoptotic cells was observed in TP53WT-expressing tumors.
source: Also, we observed an overall increase in the number of apoptotic cells in TP53WT-expressing tumors, as seen by Annexin V staining (Figure 3G; p<0.0001 Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Wild-type zebrafish tp53 when co-expressed with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish significantly suppressed tumor initiation, proliferation, and apoptosis.
source: Similarly, wild-type zebrafish tp53 when co-expressed with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish significantly suppressed tumor initiation, proliferation, and apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; p<0.0001 Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Expression of human TP53 or zebrafish tp53 selectively in ERMS using the rag2 promoter had no effect on the overall viability of zebrafish embryos or larvae.
source: Importantly, expression of human TP53WT or wild-type zebrafish tp53 selectively in ERMS using the rag2 promoter had no effect on the overall viability of zebrafish embryos or larvae.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: The TP53C176F allele is expressed by at least two ERMS patients.
source: The first selected mutation was a TP53C176F allele that is expressed by at least two ERMS patients (Chen, 2013; Seki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In one ERMS patient with TP53C176F, the second TP53 allele was deleted in the tumor and TP53C176F is present in both the primary and relapsed tumor.
source: In one of these patients, the second TP53 allele was deleted in the tumor and TP53C176F is present in both the primary and relapsed tumor (Chen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A patient with TP53P153Δ developed an aggressive refractory osteosarcoma as a teenager.
source: This patient developed an aggressive refractory osteosarcoma as a teenager, while her mother developed osteosarcoma in her early twenties; both eventually succumbed to their disease.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from a patient case.

claim: The patient's mother with TP53P153Δ developed osteosarcoma in her early twenties.
source: This patient developed an aggressive refractory osteosarcoma as a teenager, while her mother developed osteosarcoma in her early twenties; both eventually succumbed to their disease.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from a patient case.

claim: Based on the patient's family history, tumor type, and TP53 mutation, a diagnosis of Li–Fraumeni syndrome was made.
source: Based on the patient's family history, tumor type, and TP53 mutation, a diagnosis of Li–Fraumeni syndrome was made.
evidence: This is a clinical diagnosis based on patient data.

claim: p53 residue C176 is conserved across humans, mice, and zebrafish.
source: Analysis of amino acid sequence conservation showed that p53 residue C176 is conserved across humans, mice, and zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: P153 is present only in humans but is located in a region that is highly conserved across all three species.
source: P153 is present only in humans; however, it is located in a region that is highly conserved across all three species and P153 is conserved across other closely related mammalian species (Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figures.

claim: Tumor cells from the osteosarcoma patient harbored a missense mutation at c.476C>T (p.A159V).
source: Tumor cells obtained from the patient also harbored a missense mutation at c.476C>T (p.A159V) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both the SJRHB00011 PDX tumor and the primary osteosarcoma tumor expressed p53 protein.
source: Both the SJRHB00011 PDX tumor and the primary osteosarcoma tumor expressed p53 protein, as evidenced by strong positive nuclear staining in the majority of tumor cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Expression of TP53C176F with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish resulted in a significant reduction in tumor initiation compared to expressing kRASG12D alone.
source: Expression of TP53C176F with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish resulted in a significant reduction in tumor initiation compared to expressing kRASG12D alone (Figure 4H, p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS had fewer EdU-positive cells compared to tp53-/- tumors.
source: tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS had fewer EdU-positive cells but similar levels of cells undergoing mitosis compared to tp53-/- tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by EdU staining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: TP53C176F tumors showed significantly higher rates of apoptosis compared to tp53-/- tumors.
source: In contrast, TP53C176F tumors showed significantly higher rates of apoptosis (Figure 4K, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Expression of TP53P153Δ with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish did not affect tumor initiation compared to kRASG12D alone.
source: In contrast to TP53C176F-expressing ERMS, expression of TP53P153Δ with kRASG12D in tp53-/- zebrafish did not affect tumor initiation compared to kRASG12D alone (Figure 4H, p=0.774).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ-expressing zebrafish had developed twice as many ERMS in the head musculature.
source: However, unexpectedly, tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ-expressing zebrafish had developed twice as many ERMS in the head musculature (Figure 4I and J, p=0.0096, two proportions Z-test), suggesting a gain-of-function effect with respect to initiation site.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4I and 4J.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors were less proliferative compared to tp53-/-.
source: Additionally, while we did not observe a difference in apoptosis, we did find that tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors were less proliferative compared to tp53-/- (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Both tp53-/- + TP53C176F and tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors displayed increased bbc3 expression compared to tp53-/- or tp53+/+ tumors.
source: We found that both tp53-/- + TP53C176F and tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors displayed increased bbc3 expression compared to tp53-/- or tp53+/+ tumors, but had no difference with respect to cdkn1a, gadd45a and noxa expression.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53C176F and tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors expressed higher levels of cdkn1a compared to tp53+/+ ERMS.
source: We also found that tp53-/- + TP53C176F and tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ tumors expressed higher levels of cdkn1a compared to tp53+/+ ERMS
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: tp53-/- tumors express higher levels of cdkn1a compared to tp53+/+ controls.
source: however, rather unexpectedly tp53-/- tumors also express higher levels of cdkn1a compared to tp53+/+ controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ZMC1 can restore p53 activity by stabilizing mutant p53 proteins such as p53C176F.
source: It has been shown previously that ZMC1, a synthetic metallochaperone that transports zinc into cells as an ionophore, can restore p53 activity by stabilizing mutant p53 proteins such as p53C176F (Blanden et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS treated with ZMC1 showed a significant reduction in tumor growth over time compared to DMSO control.
source: Compared to DMSO-only control treatment, tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS treated with ZMC1 showed a significant reduction in tumor growth over time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and G; p=0.0116 at week 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ZMC1 treatment increased apoptosis in tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS.
source: We next assessed effects of ZMC1 on apoptosis and found increased apoptosis in tp53-/- + TP53C176F-expressing ERMS treated with ZMC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F; p=0.0008).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ZMC1 treatment increased p53C176F expression at the protein level.
source: ZMC1 treatment increased p53C176F expression at the protein level, suggesting increased stability of p53C176F protein in response to drug (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ZMC1 treatment in tp53-/- ERMS cohorts did not affect tumor growth.
source: In contrast, ZMC1 treatment in tp53-/- ERMS cohorts did not affect tumor growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and K, p=0.961)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ZMC1 treatment in tp53-/- ERMS cohorts did not affect apoptosis.
source: or apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I and J, p=0.583).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: TP53C176F appears to retain some wild-type function that partially prevents ERMS initiation in tp53-/- zebrafish.
source: Altogether, TP53C176F appears to retain some wild-type function that partially prevents ERMS initiation in tp53-/- zebrafish, as well as trigger apoptosis in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The activity of p53C176F can be further enhanced by tp53 reactivators, such as ZMC1.
source: Interestingly, the activity of p53C176F can be further enhanced by tp53 reactivators, such as ZMC1.
evidence: This is supported by the ZMC1 treatment data.

claim: Tumors expressing the TP53P153Δ have significantly fewer proliferating cells compared to tp53-/-.
source: However, tumors expressing the TP53P153Δ while having no effects on apoptosis compared to tp53-/- have significantly fewer proliferating cells, suggesting an allele with gain of function and also some wild-type activity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data.

claim: Head ERMS tumors formed in zebrafish expressing kRASG12D and TP53P153Δ in the tp53-/- background are overall less proliferative compared to trunk tumors.
source: The head ERMS tumors that are formed in zebrafish expressing kRASG12D and TP53P153Δ in the tp53-/- background initiate tumors in the head musculature around the eye and in the jaw; however, these tumors are overall less proliferative compared to the trunk tumors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: All three kRASG12D;TP53P153Δ; tp53-/-;GFP-positive tumors displayed RNA expression signatures associated with neuronal differentiation, neurotransmitter secretion, synapse formation, and neurogenesis.
source: RNAseq unexpectedly revealed that all three kRASG12D;TP53P153Δ; tp53-/-;GFP-positive tumors displayed RNA expression signatures associated with neuronal differentiation, neurotransmitter secretion, synapse formation, and neurogenesis
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data.

claim: kRASG12D; tp53-/-;GFP-positive-only tumors displayed signatures associated with myogenesis, skeletal muscle structure, and muscle differentiation.
source: while kRASG12D; tp53-/-;GFP-positive-only tumors as expected displayed signatures associated with myogenesis, skeletal muscle structure, and muscle differentiation (Figure 5A and B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: TP53P153Δ tumors had gene signatures associated with pro-neural glioblastoma, neuronal markers, and the downregulation of negative regulators of hedgehog signaling.
source: Unbiased gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) found that TP53P153Δ tumors had gene signatures associated with pro-neural glioblastoma, neuronal markers, and the downregulation of negative regulators of hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis.

claim: TP53P153Δ tumors displayed negative correlation with soft tissue tumors and glioblastomas of mesenchymal origin.
source: These tumors also displayed negative correlation with soft tissue tumors and glioblastomas of mesenchymal origin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in the figure supplement.

claim: At least some of the head tumors in TP53P153Δ-expressing zebrafish are more likely brain tumors with neuronal gene expression signatures, rather than ERMS.
source: Together, these data suggest that at least some of the head tumors are more likely brain tumors with neuronal gene expression signatures, rather than ERMS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAseq data.

claim: Approximately 20% of tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ head tumors displayed histology consistent with medulloblastoma.
source: However, we did notice that approximately 20% (5 of 24) displayed histology consistent with medulloblastoma (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: The tp53-/- group had only one zebrafish with a DsRED-positive tumor in the head with histology consistent with medulloblastoma.
source: In contrast, the tp53-/- group had only one zebrafish (1 of 20 tumors) with a DsRED-positive tumor in the head with histology consistent with medulloblastoma (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: Non-ERMS head tumors highly expressed sox10 and gfap.
source: Non-ERMS head tumors highly expressed sox10 and gfap (Supplementary file 2) and immunohistochemistry staining confirmed that these brain tumors express high levels of Sox10 and Gfap (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data and immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: None of the zebrafish expressing tp53-/- + TP53C176F initiated head tumors.
source: None of the zebrafish expressing tp53-/- + TP53C176F initiated head tumors.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Brain tumors expressing tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ were consistent with the sonic hedgehog subgroup of medulloblastomas.
source: Finally, by comparing our zebrafish brain tumors with medulloblastoma gene signatures outlined in Pomeroy et al., and Kool et al., we found that our brain tumors expressing tp53-/- + TP53P153Δ were consistent with the sonic hedgehog subgroup of medulloblastomas (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 4; Kool et al., 2014; Pomeroy et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis comparing to published medulloblastoma signatures.

claim: Deletion of P153 causes a partial narrowing of a small pocket on the surface of p53WT.
source: Homology models of p53P153Δ generated by SWISS-MODEL (Waterhouse et al., 2018) indicate that deletion of P153 causes a partial narrowing of a small pocket on the surface of p53WT (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by homology modeling shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The p53Y220C mutation causes expansion and deepening of a pocket on the p53 surface by forming a cleft bounded by L145, V147, T150-P153, P222, and P223.
source: Conversely, another known p53 mutation, the p53Y220C mutation, causes expansion and deepening of this pocket by forming a cleft bounded by L145, V147, T150-P153, P222, and P223 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mutations in P151 and P152 are present in a subset of tumors overlapping with the Y220C mutation.
source: Interestingly, mutations in P151 and P152 are present in a subset of tumors overlapping with the Y220C mutation (TCGA Research Network data; http://cancergenome.nih.gov).
evidence: This is supported by data from TCGA database.

claim: The tri-proline loop (P151-153) is mobile and can precipitate a concerted collapse of the pocket in p53Y220X mutations.
source: Previous molecular dynamics simulations of p53Y220X (X = C, H, N, or S) mutations found that the tri-proline loop (P151-153) is mobile and can precipitate a concerted collapse of the pocket, forming a frequently populated closed state and contributing to p53 instability (Bauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The TP53Y220C mutation is the ninth most frequent TP53 missense mutation.
source: The TP53Y220C mutation is the ninth most frequent TP53 missense mutation and is the most common 'conformational' TP53 mutation in cancer (Baud et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The TP53Y220C allele is frequently associated with sarcomas and head and neck carcinomas.
source: Interestingly, the TP53Y220C allele is frequently associated with sarcomas and head and neck carcinomas, and has been reported in patients with osteosarcoma and RMS (Castresana et al., 1995; Overholtzer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TP53Y220C expression inhibited ERMS initiation in tp53-/- zebrafish.
source: Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated that while TP53Y220C expression inhibited ERMS initiation (Figure 6C, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TP53Y220C expression decreased the number of primary ERMS per fish.
source: and decreased the number of primary ERMS per fish (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: TP53Y220C expression led to a significant increase in head ERMS tumors compared to tp53-/- animals.
source: TP53Y220C expression also led to a significant increase in head ERMS tumors compared to tp53-/- animals, reminiscent of tp53-/- animals expressing TP53P153Δ (Figure 6D, F and H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; 30.8% of ERMS; n = 150).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Expression TP53Y220C decreased tumor cell proliferation.
source: We also assessed TP53Y220C-expressing tumors for effects on proliferation and apoptosis and similar to tp53-/-; TP53P153Δ ERMS, expression TP53Y220C decreased tumor cell proliferation (Figure 6J, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by EdU staining data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: TP53Y220C expression led to a significant increase in apoptosis.
source: However, unlike TP53P153Δ-expressing ERMS, TP53Y220C expression led to a significant increase in apoptosis (Figure 6I, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: tp53-/- + TP53Y220C tumors expressed significantly higher gadd45a compared to tp53+/+ and tp53-/- tumors.
source: Compared to tp53+/+ and tp53-/- tumors, we found that tp53-/- + TP53Y220C tumors expressed significantly higher gadd45a, and two of three tumors expressed higher noxa and baxa but not bbc3 or cdkn1a/p21 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Two of three tp53-/- + TP53Y220C tumors expressed higher noxa and baxa.
source: Compared to tp53+/+ and tp53-/- tumors, we found that tp53-/- + TP53Y220C tumors expressed significantly higher gadd45a, and two of three tumors expressed higher noxa and baxa but not bbc3 or cdkn1a/p21 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Both the TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C mutations predispose to head ERMS tumors in zebrafish.
source: Altogether, our data reveal that both the TP53P153Δand TP53Y220C mutations predispose to head ERMS tumors in zebrafish but differ in their effects on tumor initiation, apoptosis and expression of p53 target genes noxa, baxa, bbc3 and gadd45a (SupplementarySupplementary file 1 File 1).
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Activated hedgehog signaling can initiate head and neck ERMS from a potential bipotent Kdr-positive progenitor cell in a mouse genetic model.
source: In a mouse genetic model, activated hedgehog signaling can initiate head and neck ERMS from a potential bipotent Kdr-positive progenitor cell that has endothelial and myogenic potential (Drummond et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The head ERMS tumor expressed several genes that are normally expressed in the head musculature, including tbx1, dlx3b, dlx4b, and ptch2.
source: The head ERMS tumor, while having common shared myogenic features, was distinguishable from trunk tumors and expressed several genes that are normally expressed in the head musculature, including tbx1, dlx3b, dlx4b, and ptch2 (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mutant TP53 has been shown to activate KDR expression in breast cancer cell lines.
source: Mutant TP53 has been previously shown to activate KDR expression in breast cancer cell lines (Pfister et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: High KDR expression in a subset of osteosarcoma tumors is associated with poor outcome.
source: and high KDR expression in a subset of osteosarcoma tumors is associated with poor outcome (Negri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Clinical data from the TP53P153Δ osteosarcoma patient revealed KDR amplification.
source: Clinical data from our TP53P153Δ osteosarcoma patient revealed KDR amplification.
evidence: This is clinical data from a patient case.

claim: The TP53P153Δ osteosarcoma PDX robustly expressed KDR.
source: From the patient-derived xenograft, we confirmed KDR expression using IHC analysis and using western blot found that while commonly used TP53 null osteosarcoma SaOS2 cells do not express KDR, our TP53P153Δ osteosarcoma PDX robustly expressed KDR (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by IHC and western blot data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Mosaic targeting of kdr resulted in an overall reduction in tumor initiation compared to mitfa.
source: We first assessed tumor initiation and found that mosaic targeting of kdr resulted in an overall reduction in tumor initiation compared to mitfa (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: kdr CRISPR/Cas9 resulted in a significant reduction in head ERMS tumors.
source: Importantly, kdr CRISPR/Cas9 resulted in a significant reduction in head ERMS tumors (Figure 7G–I), while targeting mitfa did not suppress head ERMS initiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7G-I.

claim: Targeting mitfa did not suppress head ERMS initiation.
source: Importantly, kdr CRISPR/Cas9 resulted in a significant reduction in head ERMS tumors (Figure 7G–I), while targeting mitfa did not suppress head ERMS initiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Efficient CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of kdr was confirmed by identifying deletions in exons 12 and 13.
source: We confirmed efficient CRISPR/Cas9 targeting using PCR, identifying deletions in exons 12 and 13, which contain the kdr catalytic domain (Figure 7J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in the figures.

claim: The data supports a role for mutant TP53P153Δ functioning in part through kdr to influence the formation of ERMS tumors in head musculature.
source: Altogether, our data supports a role for mutant TP53P153Δ functioning in part through kdr to influence the formation of ERMS tumors in head musculature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the kdr targeting experiments.

claim: The mosaic analyses are unable to distinguish whether TP53P153Δ regulation of kdr expression is required cell autonomously or in the tumor vasculature.
source: However, it is important to state that our mosaic analyses are unable to distinguish whether TP53P153Δ regulation of kdr expression is required cell autonomously or in the tumor vasculature.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: A majority of primary ERMS tumors are wild type for TP53.
source: Whole-genome/-exome/-transcriptome sequencing analysis revealed that a majority of primary ERMS tumors are wild type for TP53.
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis data.

claim: TP53 loss, mutation, or MDM2 amplification accounts for pathway disruption in approximately 30% of ERMS.
source: However, TP53 loss, mutation, or MDM2 amplification accounts for pathway disruption in approximately 30% of ERMS (Chen, 2013; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Expressing the human kRASG12D oncogene in muscle progenitor cells is sufficient to generate ERMS with morphological and molecular characteristics that recapitulate the human disease.
source: In the zebrafish ERMS model, expressing the human kRASG12D oncogene in muscle progenitor cells is sufficient to generate ERMS with morphological and molecular characteristics that recapitulate the human disease (Langenau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In a tp53 wild-type genetic background, the upper limit of tumor formation observed is 40% by 50 d post injection/fertilization in the zebrafish ERMS model.
source: Although robust, in a tp53 wild-type genetic background, the upper limit of tumor formation observed is 40% by 50 d post injection/fertilization (Langenau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Both human and zebrafish ERMS with wild-type TP53 display pathway inhibition with MDM2 amplification and/or overexpression.
source: Interestingly, both human and zebrafish ERMS with wild-type TP53 display pathway inhibition with MDM2 amplification and/or overexpression (Chen, 2013; Langenau et al., 2007; Seki et al., 2015; Shern et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TWIST1 has been shown to promote tumor initiation in sarcomas by inhibiting p53 expression.
source: Additionally, genes such as TWIST1 have been shown to promote tumor initiation in sarcomas by inhibiting p53 expression (Piccinin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mutant kRAS-induced ERMS formation increases to approximately 70% in tp53M214K/M214K mutant zebrafish.
source: Of note, mutant kRAS-induced ERMS formation increases to approximately 70% in tp53M214K/M214K mutant zebrafish (Berghmans et al., 2005; Langenau et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The tp53-/- complete loss-of-function mutant zebrafish line spontaneously forms a broader tumor spectrum than tp53M214K/M214K.
source: The tp53-/- complete loss-of-function mutant zebrafish line (Ignatius et al., 2018) spontaneously forms a broader tumor spectrum than tp53M214K/M214K, including MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, NK-cell leukemias, as well as germ cell tumors (Berghmans et al., 2005; Ignatius et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: tp53 loss specifically enhanced invasion and metastasis in vivo in ERMS.
source: Our previous work showed that tp53 loss specifically enhanced invasion and metastasis in vivo (Ignatius et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of TP53 in human ERMS may influence clinical outcomes through a combination of increased tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis.
source: suggesting that while TP53 is shown to suppress tumor progression by multiple mechanisms depending on tumor type, loss of TP53 in human ERMS may influence clinical outcomes through a combination of increased tumor cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis (Ignatius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and previous work.

claim: Human TP53 can complement wild-type tp53 function in zebrafish ERMS.
source: A second important finding is that human TP53 can complement wild-type tp53 function in zebrafish ERMS, which allows for direct study of different human variants in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing functional complementation.

claim: Both wild-type human and zebrafish Tp53 suppresses ERMS initiation and decreases proliferation in the tp53-/- background.
source: We found that both wild-type human and zebrafish Tp53 suppresses ERMS initiation and decreases proliferation in the tp53-/- background.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Higher levels of p53 induction may be required to induce apoptosis in a wild-type background.
source: However, we observed a significant increase in apoptotic cells only with overexpression, suggesting that higher levels of p53 induction may be required to induce apoptosis in a wild-type background.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The co-expression approach has been previously used to study multiple aspects of tumorigenesis in ERMS, T-ALL, melanoma, liver cancer, and neuroblastoma.
source: Our co-expression approach has been previously used to study multiple aspects of tumorigenesis in ERMS, T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL), melanoma, liver cancer, and neuroblastoma (Blackburn et al., 2014; Langenau et al., 2007; Lobbardi et al., 2017; White et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Co-expression results in protein expression comparable to or lower than p53 in human Rh30 RMS cells that endogenously express mutant p53R273C.
source: and results in protein expression comparable to or lower than p53 in human Rh30 RMS cells that endogenously express mutant p53R273C (Gibson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data and a citation.

claim: Co-expression has been an effective method to assess the role for multiple signaling pathways in ERMS, including Notch, canonical and non-canonical Wnt, Myf5, and MyoD.
source: Co-expression has been an effective method to assess the role for multiple signaling pathways in ERMS, including Notch, canonical and non-canonical Wnt, Myf5, and MyoD, with pathway validation in human cells using in vitro and in vivo methods (Chen et al., 2014b; Hayes et al., 2018; Ignatius et al., 2017; Tenente et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TP53C176F does retain some aspects of wild-type p53 function, can form tetramers with wild-type p53, and can differentially induce TP53 target gene transcription.
source: These findings are consistent with studies showing that TP53C176F does retain some aspects of wild-type p53 function, can form tetramers with wild-type p53, and can differentially induce TP53 target gene transcription (Hoffman-Luca et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Compounds like ZMC1 stabilize mutant protein to enhance p53-mediated tumor cell apoptosis and decrease growth.
source: Compounds like ZMC1 that stabilize mutant protein to enhance p53-mediated tumor cell apoptosis and decrease growth (Blanden et al., 2020; Blanden et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Chemical stabilization of the TP53C176F mutant protein could be an effective therapeutic strategy for patients with this allele.
source: Altogether, our data shows that TP53C176F is likely hypomorphic and chemical stabilization of the resulting mutant protein could be an effective therapeutic strategy for patients with this allele.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ZMC1 treatment data.

claim: The TP53P153Δ variant is rare, with only one other known patient reported.
source: In contrast to TP53C176F or TP53Y220C, the TP53P153Δ variant is rare, with only one other known patient reported (Michalarea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published case report.

claim: The patient with TP53P153Δ reported by Michalarea et al. was diagnosed with multiple tumors over several decades, including bilateral breast cancer, malignant fibrous histocytoma, and an EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
source: This patient was diagnosed with multiple tumors over several decades, including bilateral breast cancer, malignant fibrous histocytoma, and an EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
evidence: This is information from a cited case report.

claim: The patient's mother, maternal aunts, and maternal grandmother all experienced early-onset cancers, meeting the criteria for a Li–Fraumeni diagnosis.
source: The patient's mother, maternal aunts, and maternal grandmother all experienced early-onset cancers, meeting the criteria for a Li–Fraumeni diagnosis (Michalarea et al., 2014).
evidence: This is information from a cited case report.

claim: The specific Proline 153 residue is not conserved in mice or zebrafish.
source: The specific Proline 153 residue, while in a region that is highly conserved across mammalian species (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), is not conserved in mice or zebrafish
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Genetic testing done through Invitae could not assign pathogenicity to TP53P153Δ.
source: Due to its rarity in the literature and lack of animal models, genetic testing done through Invitae, a medical genetic testing provider, could not assign pathogenicity to TP53P153Δ
evidence: This is information about clinical genetic testing results.

claim: The family experience strongly suggested that TP53P153Δ is a Li–Fraumeni variant.
source: however, the family experience strongly suggested that this is a Li–Fraumeni variant.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations.

claim: The patient's osteosarcoma with TP53P153Δ was extremely aggressive and refractory to multiple anticancer agents.
source: Clinically, the patient's osteosarcoma was extremely aggressive and refractory to multiple anticancer agents.
evidence: This is a clinical observation.

claim: No other gene or pathway has been identified in the zebrafish model that predisposes to head tumors besides TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C.
source: Currently, no other gene or pathway has been identified in the zebrafish model that predisposes to head tumors, with both TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C expression in zebrafish leading to an increase in head ERMS.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the zebrafish model.

claim: Brain tumors have not been observed in rag2:kRASG12D-induced ERMS model.
source: Unexpectedly, approximately 20% of tp53-/- zebrafish expressing TP53P153Δ also develop medulloblastoma-like tumors with gene signatures consistent with the sonic hedgehog subgroup. Brain tumors have not been observed in rag2:kRASG12D –induced ERMS model
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: No brain tumors were identified in TP53Y220C or TP53C176F experimental groups.
source: and we did not identify any brain tumors in our TP53Y220C or TP53C176F experimental groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: One medulloblastoma-like tumor was identified in tp53-/- zebrafish.
source: We did identify however one medulloblastoma-like tumor in tp53-/- zebrafish.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Removal of ERMS burdened animals from the experiment before 30 days precludes study of additional tumor types in tp53-/- animals.
source: Given the rapid onset of ERMS is our model, it is possible that medulloblastoma requires more time to initiate and that removal of ERMS burdened animals from the experiment before 30 days precludes study of additional tumor types in tp53-/- animals.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Tumors in the tp53-/- + TP53C176F group grew slowly and experimental animals were followed for up to 90 days.
source: Tumors in the tp53-/- + TP53C176F group grew slowly and experimental animals were followed for up to 90 days, yet no medulloblastoma tumors were observed
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Hypomorphic TP53P153Δ activity is likely not sufficient to initiate medulloblastoma tumors, in addition to head and neck ERMS.
source: suggesting that hypomorphic TP53P153Δ activity is likely not sufficient to initiate medulloblastoma tumors, in addition to head and neck ERMS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Head and neck ERMS represent a significant proportion of all ERMS diagnoses.
source: Head and neck ERMS represent a significant proportion of all ERMS diagnoses, with the basis of regional predispositions not fully understood.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: Expression of activated Smoothened protein in mice under the control of the Ap2 promoter results primarily in head and neck ERMS that arise from Kdr-positive endothelial cells.
source: Expression of activated Smoothened protein in mice under the control of the Ap2 promoter results primarily in head and neck ERMS that arise from Kdr-positive endothelial cells (Hatley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Smoothened is a key component of the hedgehog signaling pathway that is commonly activated in ERMS.
source: Smoothened is a key component of the hedgehog signaling pathway that is commonly activated in ERMS (Drummond et al., 2018; Satheesha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The cell of origin plays a major role in ERMS initiation.
source: Modeling in mice indicates that the cell of origin plays a major role in initiation, given that activated Smoothened under the control of a more ubiquitously expressed promoter leads to ERMS tumors in other skeletal muscle populations (Mao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A recent analysis found a higher proportion of head and neck RMS tumors have TP53 mutations.
source: Importantly, a recent analysis of TP53 in RMS found a higher proportion of head and neck RMS tumors have TP53 mutations (Shern et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Differential features of TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C may predispose patients to head ERMS via regulation of kdr expression.
source: Our data suggests that differential features of TP53P153Δ and TP53Y220C may predispose patients to head ERMS via regulation of kdr expression, providing additional mechanistic insights into anatomical differences in sarcoma initiation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Certain TP53 variants may predispose individuals to head and neck rhabdomyosarcoma tumors.
source: Therefore, certain TP53 variants may predispose individuals to head and neck rhabdomyosarcoma tumors
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The cell of origin for zebrafish head ERMS remains to be identified.
source: however, the cell of origin for zebrafish head ERMS remains to be identified, as well as whether mutant TP53 interacts with hedgehog pathway signaling in head ERMS and medulloblastoma.
evidence: This is a statement about what remains unknown.

claim: In Li–Fraumeni patients, TP53 mutations are germline with somatic modifier mutations occurring secondarily.
source: In Li–Fraumeni patients, TP53 mutations are germline with somatic modifier mutations occurring secondarily.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: In the zebrafish experiments, kRASG12D and the human TP53 variant allele are introduced at the same time under the control of the rag2 promoter.
source: In our experiments, while our starting point is a tp53-/- null background, kRASG12D and the human TP53 variant allele are introduced at the same time under the control of the rag2 promoter.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Effects of mutant TP53 in the tumor microenvironment are missed in the zebrafish assays.
source: A second limitation is that effects of mutant TP53 in the tumor microenvironment are missed in our assays.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Generation of zebrafish strains with germline knock-in of equivalent mutations takes an average of 2 years for full assessment.
source: However, our assay is rapid, given that the generation of zebrafish strains with germline knock-in of the equivalent mutations takes an average of 2 years for full assessment.
evidence: This is a statement about the time required for alternative approaches.

claim: In mice, only the most common Tp53 variants have been fully characterized.
source: In mice, only the most common Tp53 variants have been fully characterized, and prioritizing which TP53 mutants to model is a challenge given cost and time restraints.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of mouse modeling.

claim: The mosaic assay bridges a gap, especially for sarcomas where the majority of TP53 mutations remain uncharacterized.
source: Our mosaic assay bridges a gap, especially for sarcomas where the majority of TP53 mutations remain uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the zebrafish model.

claim: Expression of three different patient TP53 variants leads to very different effects on tumor formation.
source: Our finding that expression of three different patient TP53 variants leads to very different effects on tumor formation highlights the importance of in vivo precision modeling
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The zebrafish ERMS model can be effective in defining multiple aspects of p53 tumor suppressor function.
source: In summary, we highlight that the zebrafish ERMS model can be effective in defining multiple aspects of p53 tumor suppressor function and delineating a spectrum of null, partial loss- and gain-of-function mutational effects in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the study.
